name: Homer

claims.text: The Iliad and Odyssey emerged from a long oral tradition using formulaic composition.
The poems reached something close to their present form in the 8th–7th centuries BC.
Some objects described in the poems reflect genuine Bronze Age material culture.
A single poet named Homer composed both epics.
Homer was a blind bard from Chios.

summary: The name attached to the Iliad and the Odyssey — the foundational poems of Greek literature, and the closest thing the Greek world had to scripture.
significance: Homeric epic supplied Greeks with a shared heroic past, a common poetic language, and the moral vocabulary that tragedy and philosophy argued with for centuries.
body:
Nothing certain is known about Homer, and there may never have been a single person. Seven cities claimed him; the ancient tradition made him a blind bard from Chios or Smyrna. What the poems demonstrably contain is an oral tradition: Milman Parry showed in the 1930s that their formulaic epithets ("swift-footed Achilles", "wine-dark sea") are the working technique of singers composing in performance, tested against living South Slavic oral poets.

The poems preserve a stratified world. Bronze Age objects — the boar's-tusk helmet, the tower shield, Nestor's cup — sit beside Iron Age cremation and Geometric-era social structures. They are not a record of the Mycenaean age but a memory of it, reshaped over four centuries of retelling.

name: Hesiod

claims.text: The Theogony and Works and Days are the work of a single identifiable poetic persona.
The Greek succession myth shows structural borrowing from Near Eastern models.
Hesiod was roughly contemporary with the composition of the Homeric poems.

summary: A Boeotian farmer-poet whose Theogony organised the Greek gods into a genealogy, and whose Works and Days is the first personal voice in European literature.
significance: Gave Greek religion a systematic cosmogony and supplied the myth of the Five Ages, the Prometheus story and Pandora in their canonical forms.
body:
Unlike Homer, Hesiod tells us about himself: his father emigrated from Aeolian Cyme to the "miserable village" of Ascra, and his brother Perses cheated him in an inheritance dispute settled by corrupt "bribe-swallowing kings". Works and Days is addressed to that brother — part farming almanac, part moral protest.

The Theogony traces the cosmos from Chaos through Gaia and Ouranos to the reign of Zeus, in a succession myth with clear parallels in the Hittite Song of Kumarbi and Babylonian Enuma Elish — evidence of Near Eastern influence on early Greek thought.

name: Sappho

claims.text: Sappho composed monodic lyric poetry on Lesbos in the late 7th and early 6th centuries BC.
Her surviving corpus is overwhelmingly fragmentary, largely recovered from papyri.
Her poetry expresses erotic desire directed at women.
Sappho led a formal circle or school of young women.
Sappho leapt to her death from the Leucadian cliff.

summary: The most celebrated lyric poet of antiquity, whose songs of desire and loss survive almost entirely in fragments.
significance: Turned Greek poetry from public narrative to interior feeling. Plato reportedly called her the tenth Muse.
body:
Sappho composed monodic lyric for performance with the lyre, in a metre now named Sapphic after her. Of nine ancient books, one nearly complete poem survives — the Hymn to Aphrodite — plus several hundred fragments, many recovered from Egyptian papyrus rubbish heaps at Oxyrhynchus. New fragments were still being published in 2014.

Her poems address women by name with unmistakable erotic intensity, which is the origin of the words *sapphic* and *lesbian*. Ancient biographical traditions about her — the leap from the Leucadian cliff for love of the ferryman Phaon — are late fiction.

name: Solon

claims.text: Solon abolished debt-slavery for Athenian citizens.
Solon replaced birth with property qualification for holding office.
Fragments of Solon's own political poetry survive.
Solon redistributed land.

summary: Athenian lawgiver of 594 BC who cancelled debts, abolished debt-slavery and opened political office by wealth rather than birth.
significance: His reforms broke the aristocratic monopoly on Athenian politics and laid the legal groundwork that Cleisthenes later turned into democracy.
body:
Solon was appointed archon with extraordinary powers during a crisis in which impoverished Athenians were being enslaved for debt on their own land. His *seisachtheia* ("shaking off of burdens") cancelled these debts and freed those enslaved by them, and he banned debt-bondage outright.

He replaced birth with property as the qualification for office, dividing citizens into four census classes, and gave every citizen — including the poorest *thetes* — the right to sit on appeal juries and to bring a prosecution on another's behalf. Then he left Athens for ten years so he could not be pressed to amend the laws. He is one of the few Greek statesmen whose own poetry survives, defending his refusal to satisfy either rich or poor completely.

name: Peisistratus

claims.text: Peisistratus ruled Athens as tyrant, with interruptions, from 561 to 527 BC.
The City Dionysia acquired its dramatic competitions under the Peisistratids.
Peisistratus commissioned an official written text of Homer.

summary: Tyrant of Athens who seized power three times and, paradoxically, strengthened the institutions that later made democracy possible.
significance: His public building, festival patronage and rural courts weakened the regional aristocracies whose power Cleisthenes would finally dismantle.
body:
Peisistratus took power in 561 BC, was twice expelled, and finally ruled securely from 546 until his death. Herodotus tells the story of his second return: he entered Athens with a tall woman dressed as Athena in a chariot, and the Athenians accepted the divine endorsement.

He expanded the Panathenaic festival, gave the City Dionysia its competitive dramatic contests, sent circuit judges into the countryside, and struck the first substantial Athenian silver coinage. The tradition that he had the Homeric poems fixed in an official text is later and uncertain. His son Hippias ruled harshly after Hipparchus was assassinated, and was expelled in 510 BC.

name: Cleisthenes

claims.text: Cleisthenes reorganised Attica into ten tribes composed of dispersed trittyes in 508/7 BC.
The Council of 500 was created as part of these reforms.
Cleisthenes introduced ostracism.

summary: Architect of the Athenian democratic constitution in 508/7 BC, who rebuilt the citizen body from scratch to break the power of regional clans.
significance: Created the institutional machinery — ten artificial tribes, the Council of 500, the deme registry — that made mass self-government workable.
body:
Cleisthenes' central move was ingenious social engineering. He divided Attica into three zones — city, coast and inland — split each into thirty units called *trittyes*, and built ten new tribes by combining one trittys from each zone. Every tribe therefore contained citizens from across Attica with no shared local loyalty, which severed the link between aristocratic families and their regional power bases.

Citizenship was registered through the *deme*, the local village or ward, and a man's demotic replaced his father's name in official use — replacing lineage with residence as the mark of identity. The Council of 500, fifty from each tribe chosen by lot, set the assembly's agenda.

name: Draco

claims.text: Draco produced Athens' first written law code, traditionally dated 621/0 BC.
A 409/8 BC re-inscription of Draco's homicide law survives.
Draco's code prescribed death for almost all offences.

summary: Author of Athens' first written law code in 621 BC — famously severe, and the origin of the word "draconian".
significance: Writing the law down took its interpretation out of the exclusive hands of aristocratic judges, however harsh its content.
body:
Ancient tradition held that Draco prescribed death for almost every offence, and that his laws were written in blood rather than ink. Solon repealed nearly all of them.

The exception is the homicide law, which survived and was re-inscribed in 409/8 BC — a copy of that inscription still exists. It is notably sophisticated: it distinguishes intentional from unintentional killing, sets out procedures for exile and pardon by the victim's family, and takes blood vengeance out of private hands. Its public display also made a rule available for scrutiny beyond an aristocratic judge's memory. The written code, not its proverbial severity, was the lasting achievement.

name: Lycurgus of Sparta

claims.text: Spartans attributed their constitution and social system to a lawgiver named Lycurgus.
The Spartan system developed gradually rather than being designed at once.
Lycurgus was a single historical individual.

summary: The legendary lawgiver to whom Spartans attributed their entire social and military system.
significance: Whether or not he existed, "Lycurgus" is how Spartans explained and legitimised the most distinctive society in Greece.
body:
Plutarch opens his Life by admitting that nothing about Lycurgus can be stated without contradiction — not his dates, his family, or what he did. Ancient estimates of his lifetime span four centuries.

The system credited to him — the *agoge* education, communal messes, the ban on gold and silver coinage, land divided into equal lots, the *krypteia* — was almost certainly assembled over generations. Attributing it to one inspired figure endorsed by Delphi gave it an authority no gradual process could. This is a case where the historical question ("did he exist?") matters less than the functional one ("what did believing in him do?").

name: Thales of Miletus

claims.text: Thales proposed water as the fundamental principle of things.
A solar eclipse visible in Anatolia occurred on 28 May 585 BC.
Thales successfully predicted that eclipse.

summary: The first Greek to explain nature without invoking the gods — traditionally the first philosopher and first scientist.
significance: Begins the Ionian tradition of natural explanation from which Greek science, and eventually European science, descends.
body:
Thales held that everything originates from water, and that the Earth floats on it. The specific answer is wrong; the form of the question was revolutionary. Asking what the world is made of, and expecting an answer in terms of ordinary materials rather than divine biography, is the founding move of natural philosophy.

He is credited with predicting a solar eclipse that stopped a battle between the Lydians and Medes — modern astronomy places one on 28 May 585 BC. How he could have done this is unclear, since Babylonian eclipse cycles do not straightforwardly predict local visibility. Aristotle also tells a story of Thales cornering the olive-press market to prove philosophers could get rich if they cared to.

name: Pythagoras

claims.text: Pythagoras founded a philosophical-religious community at Croton.
Pythagoreans identified numerical ratios underlying musical consonance.
The relation a²+b²=c² was known in Babylonian mathematics long before Pythagoras.
Pythagoras personally proved the theorem named after him.

summary: Founder of a religious-philosophical brotherhood in southern Italy that held number to be the substance of reality.
significance: Fused mathematics, music and mysticism into a tradition that shaped Plato profoundly and, through him, the whole Western idea of a mathematically ordered cosmos.
body:
Pythagoras left Samos for Croton around 530 BC and founded a community with strict rules — silence for initiates, communal property, dietary restrictions, and belief in the transmigration of souls. It held political power in several Italian cities before being violently suppressed.

The discovery that consonant musical intervals correspond to simple whole-number ratios (2:1, 3:2, 4:3) is the core Pythagorean insight, and appears to be genuine. The theorem bearing his name was known to Babylonian mathematicians a thousand years earlier; whether Pythagoras proved it is unknown. Because members attributed their own discoveries to the founder, separating the man from the school may be permanently impossible.

name: Themistocles

claims.text: Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend the Laurion silver on a fleet of triremes.
Athenian naval power was decisive at Salamis in 480 BC.
Themistocles later took service under the Persian king.
Ostraka bearing his name survive in quantity from the Athenian Agora.

summary: The Athenian who read the Delphic oracle's "wooden wall" as ships, built the fleet, and engineered the victory at Salamis.
significance: His naval policy created Athenian sea power — the basis of both the empire and the democracy that the poorest citizens, who rowed the ships, came to dominate.
body:
In 483 BC a rich vein of silver was struck at Laurion. Themistocles persuaded the assembly not to distribute the windfall to citizens but to build 200 triremes. Three years later that fleet met the Persian invasion.

Before Salamis he sent a servant to Xerxes with false intelligence that the Greeks were about to flee, luring the larger Persian fleet into the narrows where its numbers became a liability. The Greeks won decisively. He then rebuilt Athens' walls against Spartan objections, stalling the Spartan envoys personally while the work went on.

He was ostracised around 471 BC, condemned in absentia for treason, and ended his life as a governor in the service of the Persian king — a reversal Thucydides recounts without visible irony.

name: Leonidas I

claims.text: A Greek force under Leonidas held Thermopylae for three days in 480 BC before being outflanked.
Around 300 Spartans, with Thespians and Thebans, remained for the final stand.
Persian arrowheads and a Greek rampart have been identified near the ancient pass.
Herodotus' figures for the size of Xerxes' army are reliable.

summary: Spartan king who died with his rearguard holding the pass at Thermopylae against Xerxes' army in 480 BC.
significance: The defeat became the defining Greek story of disciplined resistance against overwhelming odds, and remains one of antiquity's most durable images.
body:
Leonidas commanded a Greek force of perhaps 7,000 at the narrow pass of Thermopylae. For two days they held. Then a local, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path around the position. Leonidas dismissed most of the army and remained with 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans.

All the Spartans and Thespians died. Simonides' epitaph, recorded by Herodotus, is the most famous couplet in Greek: it asks the passer-by to tell the Spartans that here they lie, obedient to their words. The delay bought the Greek fleet time, and the moral effect of the stand outlasted the tactical loss by two and a half millennia.

name: Pericles

claims.text: Pericles was elected strategos in most years between 461 and 429 BC.
He introduced state pay for jurors.
Delian League funds were used for the Acropolis building programme.
Pericles died of the plague in 429 BC.
The Funeral Oration records Pericles' actual words.

summary: The dominant Athenian politician for three decades, who rebuilt the Acropolis, extended democratic participation and led Athens into the Peloponnesian War.
significance: His name marks the height of Athenian power, and the buildings he commissioned remain the visual signature of Greek civilisation.
body:
Pericles was elected *strategos* — general — repeatedly from 461 BC until shortly before his death. That office, unlike almost every other, was elective and re-electable, and it was the base of his authority; he held no permanent power and had to win the assembly's vote again and again.

He introduced pay for jury service, which made participation possible for poor citizens, and moved the Delian League treasury to Athens, spending allied tribute on the Parthenon, Propylaea and Odeon. Thucydides gives him the Funeral Oration, the classic statement of Athenian democratic self-understanding, and also judges his regime "in name a democracy, but in fact rule by the first man".

His strategy at the outbreak of war — abandon the countryside, rely on the fleet, wait Sparta out — was sound and was destroyed by an unforeseeable variable. Plague broke out in the crowded city in 430 BC and killed him in 429.

name: Aspasia of Miletus

claims.text: Aspasia was a Milesian metic who lived with Pericles and bore him a son.
Contemporary comic poets attacked her repeatedly.
She taught rhetoric or influenced Athenian intellectual circles.
She ran a brothel.

summary: A Milesian woman in Pericles' household, credited by Plato and others with unusual influence on Athenian intellectual life.
significance: The best-documented non-royal woman of Classical Athens, and a test case for how thoroughly hostile male sources can distort a life.
body:
As a *metic* — a resident foreigner — Aspasia was outside the restrictions binding Athenian citizen women, which is probably why she could appear in public intellectual settings at all. Plato's *Menexenus* has Socrates claim she wrote Pericles' funeral speech, though the dialogue's tone makes it hard to read straight.

Comic poets attacked her savagely, calling her a brothel-keeper and blaming her for starting two wars. These are jokes aimed at Pericles through her, not testimony. Almost everything about her comes through such filters, and the result is a figure who is unusually visible and unusually hard to see clearly.

name: Herodotus

claims.text: Herodotus composed the Histories in the mid-5th century BC.
He explicitly distinguishes between what he was told and what he believes.
Scythian burial practices he describes have been confirmed by excavation.
His army and casualty figures are systematically exaggerated.
Herodotus personally travelled to all the places he describes.

summary: Author of the Histories, the first sustained prose enquiry into the human past — an account of the Persian Wars that ranges across the known world.
significance: Invented history as a genre: a named investigator, weighing evidence and reporting conflicting versions rather than reciting tradition.
body:
His opening sentence sets out the programme: this is the *historie* — enquiry — of Herodotus, so that human achievements are not forgotten and the reason Greeks and barbarians fought is preserved. The word *historia* means investigation; it acquires its modern sense from this book.

He travelled widely, describing Egypt, Scythia, Babylon and Libya with an ethnographic curiosity that has no precedent. His method is to report what he was told and mark his own doubt: he repeatedly says he must record what is said but is not obliged to believe it. Ancient critics called him a liar; modern archaeology has vindicated him on numerous specifics, including details of Egyptian practice and Scythian burial that once seemed fanciful.

name: Thucydides

claims.text: Thucydides was an Athenian general exiled after failing to save Amphipolis in 424 BC.
His history breaks off unfinished in 411 BC.
He excluded divine causation from historical explanation.
The speeches reproduce what was actually said.

summary: Athenian general turned historian of the Peloponnesian War, and the founder of critical, evidence-based historical method.
significance: Stripped the gods and the marvellous out of historical explanation, replacing them with power, interest and human nature — the model for political history ever since.
body:
Thucydides commanded an Athenian fleet in 424 BC, failed to relieve Amphipolis, and was exiled for twenty years. He used the time to interview participants on both sides, which is precisely why the work is not a partisan Athenian account.

He states his method explicitly: he rejects poetic embellishment, cross-checks eyewitness reports against each other, and warns his book will be less entertaining as a result. He intends it as "a possession for all time". His analysis of how war corrodes language and morality — the account of civil war at Corcyra — is still routinely cited by political scientists.

The history breaks off mid-sentence in 411 BC, seven years before the war ended.

name: Socrates

claims.text: Socrates was tried and executed in Athens in 399 BC on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth.
Socrates wrote nothing himself.
He served as a hoplite at Potidaea, Delium and Amphipolis.
As a member of the presiding council in 406 BC, he alone refused to allow the illegal mass trial of the Arginusae generals to proceed.
Plato's dialogues accurately report Socrates' own philosophy.
The trial was politically motivated by his association with the Thirty.

summary: Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing, questioned everyone, and was executed by the democracy in 399 BC.
significance: Turned philosophy from cosmology to ethics — how one ought to live — and made cross-examination the method of philosophical enquiry.
body:
Socrates spent his life in the Athenian agora asking people to define what they claimed to know: courage, piety, justice. The *elenchus* — a sequence of questions exposing contradiction in the respondent's own beliefs — is his signature method, and it made him enemies steadily.

He was tried in 399 BC for impiety and corrupting the young. The charge is inseparable from politics: Athens had just lost the war and endured the murderous rule of the Thirty Tyrants, several of whom had been in his circle. Under an amnesty they could not be prosecuted directly. He was convicted by a narrow margin, proposed free meals for life as his counter-penalty, and drank hemlock.

Everything known about him comes through others — Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes — who disagree substantially. This is the "Socratic problem".

name: Plato

claims.text: Plato founded the Academy in Athens c. 387 BC.
The complete Platonic corpus survives, along with some spurious works.
Plato travelled to Sicily and involved himself with the court of Dionysius.
The Seventh Letter is genuinely by Plato.
The Atlantis story reflects a memory of Minoan Crete or Thera.

summary: Student of Socrates, founder of the Academy, and author of the dialogues that set the agenda for Western philosophy.
significance: Whitehead's remark that European philosophy is footnotes to Plato overstates the case, but not by much: metaphysics, epistemology, ethics and political theory all take their initial shape here.
body:
Plato founded the Academy around 387 BC in a grove outside Athens — arguably the first institution of higher learning in Europe, and it operated for nearly three centuries.

His central doctrine is the theory of Forms: the changing things we perceive are imperfect instances of perfect, unchanging realities grasped by reason alone. The *Republic* builds a just city as a model for the just soul, argues for rule by philosopher-kings, and contains the Allegory of the Cave. His political proposals are genuinely authoritarian — censorship of poetry, a rigid class structure, state control of reproduction — and reading him as a straightforward democrat requires ignoring the text.

Unusually for an ancient author, his complete works survive.

name: Aristotle

claims.text: Aristotle founded the Lyceum in Athens in 335 BC.
He tutored Alexander at Mieza in Macedon.
Several of his zoological observations were confirmed only in the modern era.
The surviving works are lecture notes rather than published treatises.

summary: Plato's student, Alexander's tutor, founder of the Lyceum, and the most systematically encyclopaedic mind of antiquity.
significance: Effectively founded logic, biology, literary criticism and political science as distinct disciplines, and dominated European and Islamic thought for nearly two thousand years.
body:
Aristotle studied under Plato for twenty years, then broke with the theory of Forms: for him, form is not in a separate realm but in the thing itself. That shift turns philosophy towards empirical investigation of the world.

He collected and dissected specimens; his marine biology at Lesbos is accurate enough that some of his observations — the hectocotyl arm of the octopus, the placental dogfish — were dismissed for centuries and only confirmed in the nineteenth. He and his school also collected the constitutions of 158 cities, of which the *Constitution of the Athenians* survives on papyrus.

He tutored the young Alexander at Mieza from 343 BC. After Alexander's death, anti-Macedonian feeling forced him to leave Athens — reportedly saying he would not let the city sin twice against philosophy.

name: Aeschylus

claims.text: Aeschylus fought at the battle of Marathon in 490 BC.
The Persians (472 BC) is the earliest surviving Greek play.
The Oresteia is the only complete surviving tragic trilogy.
Aeschylus introduced the second actor to tragedy.

summary: The earliest tragedian whose plays survive, and a veteran of Marathon who put the Persian Wars on stage.
significance: Added the second actor, making genuine dramatic conflict possible, and turned tragedy into an instrument for examining justice and the divine order.
body:
Aeschylus fought at Marathon and probably Salamis; his epitaph mentioned only his military service, not his plays. His *Persians* (472 BC) is the only surviving Greek tragedy on a contemporary historical subject, and remarkably it stages the Persian defeat from the Persian court's point of view, inviting sympathy for the enemy.

The *Oresteia* (458 BC) is the only complete tragic trilogy to survive: Agamemnon murdered by Clytemnestra, Orestes' vengeance, and his trial at Athens where Athena establishes a human court to end the cycle of blood vengeance. It is a myth about the birth of law.

name: Sophocles

claims.text: Seven complete tragedies by Sophocles survive out of roughly 120 written.
Aristotle treated Oedipus Rex as the paradigm of tragic plot construction.
Sophocles held the office of general at Athens.
He introduced the third actor.

summary: Tragedian of Oedipus Rex and Antigone, who won more dramatic victories than any of his rivals and served Athens as general and priest.
significance: Perfected tragic structure — Aristotle used Oedipus Rex as his model of plot — and shifted focus from cosmic justice to individual character under pressure.
body:
Sophocles wrote around 120 plays and won first prize perhaps 24 times, never placing lower than second. Seven complete tragedies survive.

*Oedipus Rex* is the tightest plot in Greek drama: a king investigating a plague discovers he is himself the pollution, and every step towards the truth is a step towards his destruction. *Antigone* sets the unwritten law of burial against the state's edict, with neither side wholly right — Creon's claim of civic order is not simply dismissed.

He added the third actor and expanded the chorus, and held public office throughout: he was elected general, probably serving with Pericles, and was a priest of a healing cult.

name: Euripides

claims.text: Nineteen plays attributed to Euripides survive.
He won markedly fewer dramatic victories than Sophocles or Aeschylus.
The Trojan Women was produced in 415 BC, shortly after the Melian massacre.
The Trojan Women was intended as a protest against Athenian policy at Melos.

summary: The most unsettling of the tragedians, who gave voice to women, slaves and the defeated, and questioned the gods openly.
significance: His psychological realism and moral scepticism made him the least successful tragedian in his lifetime and the most read afterwards.
body:
Euripides won only four or five victories, far fewer than Sophocles, and Aristophanes mocked him relentlessly. Yet more of his plays survive than of the other two combined — nineteen — largely because they remained popular reading after his death.

*Medea* (431 BC) gives its heroine a speech on the condition of women that is unmatched in Greek literature, then has her murder her own children and escape unpunished in a divine chariot. *The Trojan Women* (415 BC), staged the year after Athens massacred the men of Melos, presents the aftermath of a sack entirely from the perspective of the enslaved women. It is very hard not to read as an indictment.

name: Aristophanes

claims.text: Eleven complete plays by Aristophanes survive.
The Clouds caricatures Socrates as a sophist and natural philosopher.
Old Comedy named and mocked living public figures at state-sponsored festivals.
The Clouds materially contributed to Socrates' conviction.

summary: Master of Old Comedy, who lampooned living Athenians — generals, philosophers, poets — by name and to their faces.
significance: The only surviving Old Comedy, and an irreplaceable window onto Athenian daily life, slang and political argument.
body:
Eleven of his plays survive. *The Clouds* (423 BC) portrays Socrates suspended in a basket studying the heavens and teaching students to argue the unjust case successfully — Plato's *Apology* has Socrates cite it as a source of the prejudice that killed him.

*Lysistrata* (411 BC) has the women of Greece withhold sex until the men make peace. *The Frogs* (405 BC) sends Dionysus to the underworld to bring back a poet who can save the city, and stages a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides that is the earliest surviving work of literary criticism.

The freedom of this comedy is itself evidence: a democracy at war permitted its most prominent citizens to be ridiculed on stage at a state religious festival.

name: Pheidias

claims.text: Pheidias directed the sculptural programme of the Parthenon.
His workshop at Olympia has been identified by excavation.
A cup inscribed "I belong to Pheidias" was found in that workshop.
No original work by Pheidias survives.

summary: Overseer of the Parthenon sculptures and maker of the colossal Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders.
significance: Defined the visual language of the Classical style — and none of his major works survives except at second hand.
body:
Pericles put Pheidias in charge of the Acropolis programme. He made the Athena Parthenos, twelve metres of gold and ivory over a wooden core, and the seated Zeus at Olympia, which Roman visitors described as capable of consoling the grieving.

Both are lost. What survives is the Parthenon frieze and pediments, made by a workshop under his direction, plus Roman copies and coin images. His workshop at Olympia has been excavated, and a plain black cup was found inside it inscribed "I belong to Pheidias" — one of the most direct personal traces of any ancient artist.

He was prosecuted, apparently for embezzling gold from the Athena statue, though the charge may have been an attack on Pericles through him.

name: Hippocrates

claims.text: The Hippocratic Corpus is a compilation by multiple authors.
On the Sacred Disease argues explicitly against supernatural causation of epilepsy.
Hippocratic physicians recorded detailed longitudinal case observations.
Hippocrates wrote the Oath.

summary: The physician of Kos whose name attaches to a body of medical writing that separated disease from divine punishment.
significance: Established medicine as a discipline based on observation, prognosis and ethical obligation rather than religious healing.
body:
The Hippocratic Corpus is around sixty works by many hands over more than a century; how much Hippocrates himself wrote is unknown. What unifies it is a naturalistic stance. *On the Sacred Disease* attacks the idea that epilepsy is divine: it has a natural cause like every other illness, and those who call it sacred are concealing their ignorance.

The clinical case histories in the *Epidemics* are careful daily observations that often end with the patient dying — recorded anyway, because the point was to learn the course of disease. The Oath, with its commitments to confidentiality and to doing no harm, remains the ancestor of medical ethics, though it is unlikely to be by Hippocrates.

The underlying humoral theory was wrong, and it dominated European medicine for two thousand years.

name: Alcibiades

claims.text: Alcibiades promoted the Sicilian Expedition and was recalled to face charges in 415 BC.
He defected to Sparta and advised the fortification of Decelea.
He was later recalled to Athenian command and won naval victories.
Alcibiades was responsible for the mutilation of the herms.

summary: Brilliant, treacherous Athenian aristocrat who commanded for Athens, defected to Sparta, advised Persia, and returned to Athens again.
significance: His career is the clearest single illustration of how personal ambition destabilised Athenian democracy during the Peloponnesian War.
body:
Alcibiades pushed Athens into the Sicilian Expedition in 415 BC. On the eve of departure the city's herms were mutilated overnight; he was implicated, recalled for trial, and instead defected to Sparta — where he advised them to fortify Decelea in Attica permanently, which did Athens enormous harm.

He then fell out with the Spartans, moved to the Persian satrap Tissaphernes, and negotiated his own return to Athens, winning naval victories before a subordinate's defeat gave his enemies the pretext to remove him. He was assassinated in Phrygia in 404 BC.

He was also a close associate of Socrates, who saved his life at Potidaea. Plato's *Symposium* gives him a drunken speech of genuine love for Socrates, and his association with the philosopher counted against Socrates at trial.

name: Xenophon

claims.text: Xenophon marched with the Ten Thousand and wrote a first-person account of the retreat.
Cyrus the Younger was killed at Cunaxa in 401 BC.
The Hellenica continues Greek history from where Thucydides stops.
The Anabasis influenced later Macedonian strategy against Persia.

summary: Soldier, student of Socrates and author of the Anabasis — the first-person account of ten thousand Greek mercenaries fighting their way out of Persia.
significance: Wrote the earliest surviving military memoir, and provides the main continuation of Greek history after Thucydides breaks off.
body:
Xenophon joined a mercenary army hired by Cyrus the Younger to overthrow his brother, the Persian king. Cyrus was killed at Cunaxa in 401 BC and the Greek generals were seized under truce and executed. Stranded a thousand miles inside hostile territory, the survivors elected new commanders — Xenophon among them — and marched north through Armenian winter to the Black Sea. Their shout of "Thalatta! Thalatta!" — the sea, the sea — on first sighting it is among the most famous moments in Greek literature.

He later fought for Sparta, was exiled from Athens, and wrote widely: the *Hellenica*, Socratic memoirs, a treatise on horsemanship and one on estate management. His demonstration that a Greek army could operate deep inside Persia was not lost on Philip and Alexander.

name: Lysander

claims.text: Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BC.
Persian subsidies funded the Spartan fleet.
He installed the Thirty Tyrants at Athens in 404 BC.

summary: The Spartan admiral who destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami and ended the Peloponnesian War.
significance: Won the war by building, with Persian money, the one thing Sparta had always lacked: a fleet.
body:
Lysander secured funding from the Persian prince Cyrus the Younger — an alliance that traded the Greek cities of Asia Minor back to Persian control in exchange for the ships that beat Athens.

At Aegospotami in 405 BC he caught the Athenian fleet beached and unprepared and captured nearly all of it. Athens, dependent on imported grain through the Hellespont, was starved into surrender within months. The Long Walls were pulled down to flute music.

He installed narrow oligarchies backed by Spartan garrisons across the former empire, including the Thirty Tyrants at Athens. He was reportedly the first living Greek to receive divine honours from cities.

name: Epaminondas

claims.text: Epaminondas defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC using a massed left wing.
He liberated Messenia and refounded Messene as an independent city.
Spartan power declined permanently after Leuctra.
Philip II learned Macedonian tactics while a hostage at Thebes.

summary: Theban general who broke Spartan military supremacy at Leuctra in 371 BC and freed the Messenian helots.
significance: Ended Sparta as a great power permanently, and pioneered the tactical asymmetry that Philip II — a hostage in Thebes as a youth — would later develop.
body:
At Leuctra, Epaminondas massed his left wing fifty ranks deep against the Spartan right, held back the rest of his line, and shattered the elite before the weaker Theban centre and right were engaged. It was the first clear use of a deliberately unequal battle line, and roughly 400 of the 700 Spartiates present were killed — a demographic wound Sparta could not absorb.

He then invaded the Peloponnese and did the decisive thing: he liberated Messenia, whose helots had farmed the land that fed the Spartan military system for three centuries. He refounded Messene as a fortified city. Sparta never recovered.

He was killed at Mantinea in 362 BC, and Theban hegemony died with him.

name: Demosthenes

claims.text: Demosthenes delivered a series of speeches opposing Philip II of Macedon.
He negotiated the Athenian-Theban alliance that fought at Chaeronea.
He died by suicide in 322 BC after the failure of the Lamian War.
He accepted money from Persia to oppose Macedon.

summary: The greatest Athenian orator, who spent his career warning that Philip of Macedon meant to end Greek freedom — and was right.
significance: His speeches are the finest surviving Greek oratory and the fullest contemporary record of resistance to Macedon.
body:
Plutarch reports that Demosthenes overcame a speech impediment by declaiming with pebbles in his mouth and speaking over the noise of waves. The story is probably embroidered; the intensity of preparation it describes is consistent with the speeches.

The *Philippics* and *Olynthiacs* argue relentlessly that Philip is not a conventional rival but an existential threat, and that Athenians must fund and serve in campaigns themselves rather than hiring mercenaries. He assembled the Theban alliance that fought at Chaeronea in 338 BC and lost.

After Alexander's death he supported a final revolt. When it failed he took poison in a temple of Poseidon rather than be captured. He was, on the central question, correct and unsuccessful.

name: Isocrates

claims.text: Isocrates advocated a Panhellenic campaign against Persia under a single leader.
He addressed a published appeal to Philip II in 346 BC.
He starved himself to death after learning of Chaeronea.

summary: Athenian teacher of rhetoric who urged the Greeks to unite under a strong leader and invade Persia — and looked to Philip II to do it.
significance: Formulated the Panhellenic ideology that Philip and Alexander used to justify the conquest of Persia.
body:
Isocrates had a weak voice and never spoke in the assembly; he taught and published instead, and his school shaped Greek education for centuries. His *Panegyricus* (380 BC) argued that Greek unity could only be achieved against a common enemy.

In the *Address to Philip* (346 BC) he named the man: Philip should reconcile the leading cities and lead a united campaign into Asia. Whether this made him a visionary or a collaborator has been argued ever since — Demosthenes was making exactly the opposite case at exactly the same time.

He reportedly died shortly after Chaeronea, aged 98.

name: Philip II of Macedon

claims.text: Philip II reformed the Macedonian army around the sarissa phalanx and Companion cavalry.
He defeated the Greek coalition at Chaeronea in 338 BC and formed the League of Corinth.
He was assassinated by Pausanias at Aegae in 336 BC.
He lost his right eye to an arrow at the siege of Methone.
Tomb II at Vergina is his burial.
Olympias or Alexander instigated the assassination.

summary: The king who reforged Macedon's army, subdued Greece at Chaeronea, and planned the invasion of Persia his son carried out.
significance: Built the instrument of conquest. Alexander's campaigns are inconceivable without Philip's army, treasury and diplomatic groundwork.
body:
Philip took a broken kingdom in 359 BC and made it the strongest power in Europe within two decades. The military reforms were fundamental: the sarissa pike phalanx, the Companion Cavalry as a shock arm, professional year-round soldiers, and a siege train with torsion catapults.

He was also a formidable diplomat and a systematic briber — Demosthenes complained that no fortress was impregnable if a mule loaded with silver could reach the gate. He married at least seven times, each marriage a treaty.

He paid physically: he lost an eye at Methone, and his skeleton would be expected to show a severe leg wound. In 336 BC, at the wedding of his daughter, he was killed by his bodyguard Pausanias. Whether Olympias or Alexander was involved has never been settled.

name: Alexander the Great

claims.text: Alexander defeated the Achaemenid Empire in campaigns between 334 and 330 BC.
He founded Alexandria in Egypt in 331 BC.
He reached the Hyphasis river in the Punjab, where his army refused to continue.
He died in Babylon in June 323 BC.
He was poisoned.
He died of malaria, typhoid or complications of alcohol and untreated wounds.
He believed himself divine, or the son of Zeus-Ammon.

summary: King of Macedon who destroyed the Achaemenid Empire in a decade of campaigning, reached the Indus, and died at 32 without an heir.
significance: Redrew the political map from the Adriatic to the Punjab and made Greek the language of government and learning across the Near East for a thousand years.
body:
Alexander became king at twenty, immediately suppressed revolts in Greece — destroying Thebes as an example — and crossed into Asia in 334 BC. He won at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, took Tyre by building a causeway to an island city, was crowned in Egypt, and burned Persepolis.

He kept going: through Bactria and Sogdiana, over the Hindu Kush, into the Punjab, where he beat Porus and his elephants at the Hydaspes in monsoon rain. At the Hyphasis his men refused to march further. The return through Gedrosia killed thousands.

He was not simply a conqueror on the Greek model. He kept Persian administrators, adopted elements of Persian ceremonial, and married Roxana and then Darius' daughter. He also killed his friend Cleitus in a drunken quarrel and had Parmenion murdered. He died in Babylon in 323 BC after eleven days of fever, and his empire was fought over within hours.

name: Olympias

claims.text: Olympias was a Molossian princess of Epirus who married Philip II.
She held military and political power in Macedon during the succession wars.
She was executed on Cassander's orders in 316 BC.
She was involved in Philip II's assassination.
Hostile ancient portrayals of her exaggerate her cruelty and fanaticism.

summary: Molossian princess, wife of Philip II, mother of Alexander, and a ruthless political operator in the succession wars after his death.
significance: One of the few women in Greek history who exercised open political and military power, and was executed for it.
body:
Olympias came from the royal house of Epirus and claimed descent from Achilles — a lineage Alexander took seriously. Ancient sources describe her involvement in ecstatic Dionysiac religion, including handling snakes, though these accounts come from writers hostile to her.

After Philip took another wife she was sidelined, and after his murder she was widely suspected of involvement. During the wars of the Diadochi she invaded Macedon, captured and executed Philip III Arrhidaeus and his wife Eurydice, and was besieged by Cassander at Pydna. She surrendered on terms and was killed anyway in 316 BC, reportedly by relatives of those she had executed, since Cassander's soldiers refused to do it.

name: Hephaestion

claims.text: Hephaestion held the office of chiliarch, second to Alexander.
He died at Ecbatana in 324 BC and received extraordinary funeral honours.
Ancient authors likened him and Alexander to Patroclus and Achilles.
The two were lovers.

summary: Alexander's closest companion and second-in-command, whose sudden death at Ecbatana provoked an extraordinary public crisis of grief.
significance: The relationship is the best-attested personal bond in Alexander's life and shaped his behaviour at key moments.
body:
Hephaestion grew up with Alexander and rose to *chiliarch*, the second office in the empire. At Susa in 324 BC he married Drypetis, sister of Alexander's own bride Stateira, so their children would be cousins.

He died at Ecbatana later that year. Alexander's response was extravagant even by his standards: he reportedly lay on the body for a day, cut his hair, executed the physician, banned music, and ordered a monumental pyre at Babylon at enormous cost. He asked the oracle at Siwa whether Hephaestion could be worshipped as a god and settled for hero cult.

Ancient sources compared the pair to Achilles and Patroclus, and Alexander did visit their supposed tombs at Troy together. Whether the relationship was sexual is not stated in the surviving sources and cannot be resolved.

name: Parmenion

claims.text: Parmenion commanded the left wing in Alexander's major battles.
He was killed on Alexander's orders in 330 BC after his son Philotas was executed.
Philotas was genuinely guilty of conspiracy.

summary: Philip II's most senior general, who served Alexander as second-in-command until Alexander had him killed.
significance: Represents the older Macedonian establishment whose loyalty Alexander eventually found incompatible with his own transformation.
body:
Parmenion commanded the left wing at Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela — the defensive anchor while Alexander struck from the right. Arrian repeatedly has him counsel caution and Alexander overrule him, a pattern probably shaped by later sources wanting a foil for Alexander's boldness.

In 330 BC his son Philotas was accused of failing to report a plot, tortured, and executed. Alexander then sent riders ahead to Ecbatana to kill Parmenion before news could reach him. There was no evidence against him. It is the clearest case of Alexander eliminating a potential rival on grounds of position rather than proof.

name: Ptolemy I Soter

claims.text: Ptolemy took control of Egypt after Alexander's death and founded a dynasty.
He diverted Alexander's funeral procession to Egypt.
He founded the Museum and Library of Alexandria.
His lost history of Alexander was Arrian's main source.

summary: Alexander's general and bodyguard who seized Egypt, hijacked his corpse, founded a dynasty that lasted three centuries, and created the Library of Alexandria.
significance: Built the most stable and intellectually productive of the successor kingdoms, ruled by his descendants until Cleopatra VII.
body:
Ptolemy took Egypt as his satrapy in 323 BC and made it a kingdom. His most audacious move was to intercept Alexander's funeral cortege on its way to Macedon and divert it to Egypt — possession of the body conferred enormous legitimacy, and it became the centrepiece of a shrine in Alexandria.

He founded the Museum and Library, importing scholars on salary and pursuing an aggressive acquisition policy: ships docking at Alexandria had their books copied, with the copies returned and originals retained. He also created the syncretic god Serapis to give Greeks and Egyptians a shared cult.

He wrote a history of Alexander's campaigns, now lost, which was Arrian's principal source — so much of what we know about Alexander reaches us through his general's account.

name: Seleucus I Nicator

claims.text: Seleucus founded the Seleucid Empire, the largest successor state.
The Seleucid Era dating system begins in 312/311 BC and was used for centuries.
He exchanged eastern territory with Chandragupta Maurya for war elephants.
His elephants were decisive at the battle of Ipsus in 301 BC.

summary: Founder of the Seleucid Empire, the largest of Alexander's successor states, stretching from Anatolia to Central Asia.
significance: Ruled the greatest territorial share of Alexander's conquests and planted Greek cities across Mesopotamia, Iran and beyond.
body:
Seleucus was made satrap of Babylonia in 321 BC, driven out, and returned in 312 — a date the Seleucid Era counts from, making it the first continuous numbered year-count in history and the ancestor of all such systems.

He pushed east to the Indus and met Chandragupta Maurya. Rather than fight, he ceded the easternmost provinces in exchange for 500 war elephants — which proved decisive at Ipsus in 301 BC. He founded Antioch and Seleucia-on-the-Tigris and married the Sogdian noblewoman Apama, whose son Antiochus I succeeded him. He was assassinated in 281 BC while attempting to take Macedon, the one prize he never got.

name: Archimedes

claims.text: Archimedes established the law of the lever and the principle of buoyancy.
He determined the relationship between the volumes of a sphere and its circumscribing cylinder.
The Archimedes Palimpsest preserves otherwise lost works including The Method.
He was killed during the Roman sack of Syracuse in 212 BC.
He set Roman ships on fire using mirrors.
He shouted "Eureka" on discovering the principle of buoyancy in the bath.

summary: The greatest mathematician and engineer of antiquity — founder of hydrostatics, and the man who came closest to inventing calculus.
significance: His method of exhaustion anticipates integration by nearly two millennia, and his mechanics remained unsurpassed until the seventeenth century.
body:
Archimedes determined the value of π between 3¹⁰/₇₁ and 3¹/₇, found the volume and surface area of the sphere in terms of the circumscribing cylinder — he asked for that diagram on his tomb — and established the law of the lever and the principle of buoyancy.

His siege engines defended Syracuse against the Romans for two years: cranes that lifted ships out of the water, and catapults ranged for every distance. The "burning mirrors" story is late and physically doubtful.

He was killed in 212 BC by a Roman soldier during the sack, reportedly while working on a diagram. In 1906 a medieval prayer book was found to be a palimpsest over erased Archimedes texts, including *The Method*, in which he explains how he used mechanical reasoning and indivisibles to discover results before proving them rigorously.

name: Euclid

claims.text: The Elements systematises Greek geometry from a small set of postulates.
It remained a standard mathematics textbook into the 20th century.
The parallel postulate is independent of the other four.
Euclid was a single individual rather than a group of authors.

summary: Author of the Elements, the most influential textbook ever written and the model of deductive reasoning for two thousand years.
significance: Established the axiomatic method: a handful of definitions and postulates, from which everything else is proved.
body:
Almost nothing is known about Euclid's life. The *Elements* organises the mathematics of his predecessors into thirteen books proceeding from five postulates. It was used as a school text into the twentieth century — only the Bible has been printed in more editions.

Book IX contains the proof that there are infinitely many primes, still a model of elegant argument. The fifth postulate, about parallel lines, is noticeably less self-evident than the others; attempts to derive it from the rest failed for two millennia, and in the nineteenth century Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Riemann showed why — dropping it produces consistent non-Euclidean geometries, which turned out to describe physical spacetime.

Asked by Ptolemy for a shorter route to geometry, he is said to have replied that there is no royal road.

name: Eratosthenes

claims.text: Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference from the angle of shadows at two locations.
He served as chief librarian at Alexandria.
He devised the prime-number sieve named after him.
His result was within a few percent of the true value.

summary: Chief librarian at Alexandria who measured the circumference of the Earth using shadows, and effectively invented geography.
significance: Demonstrated that a global physical quantity could be determined by measurement and reasoning from a single location.
body:
Eratosthenes knew that at noon on the summer solstice the sun shone straight down a well at Syene, casting no shadow. At Alexandria on the same day a vertical gnomon cast a shadow at about 1/50th of a circle — 7.2°. If the Earth is a sphere and the sun's rays effectively parallel, then the distance between the cities is 1/50th of the circumference. He multiplied by 50 and got roughly 250,000 stades.

How accurate that is depends on which stade he used; on the most likely value the error is under 2%. Either way the method is impeccable, and he was working with a measured road distance and a stick.

He also produced a world map with parallels and meridians, calculated the tilt of the ecliptic, and devised the sieve for finding prime numbers that still bears his name. Rivals nicknamed him "Beta" for being second-best at everything — which, given the range, was a compliment in disguise.

name: Aristarchus of Samos

claims.text: Aristarchus proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun.
His heliocentric argument is known chiefly through Archimedes' summary.
The absence of observable stellar parallax was a principal ancient objection to heliocentrism.
His treatise on the sizes and distances of the Sun and Moon survives.

summary: The first person known to have placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre of the cosmos — eighteen centuries before Copernicus.
significance: Proposed heliocentrism with a coherent supporting argument, and was set aside for reasons that were, on the evidence then available, defensible.
body:
Aristarchus' heliocentric proposal survives only because Archimedes summarised it in *The Sand Reckoner*. He also argued that the sphere of fixed stars was immensely larger than previously supposed — a necessary consequence, since no stellar parallax could be observed.

That was precisely the objection. If the Earth moves, nearby stars should shift against distant ones over the year. No such shift was detectable, so either the stars were unimaginably far away or the Earth was still. Ancient astronomers reasonably chose the second. Stellar parallax was not measured until 1838.

His surviving treatise on the sizes and distances of the Sun and Moon uses sound geometry with imprecise measurements, and gets the Sun about twenty times too close — but establishes correctly that it is much larger than the Earth.

name: Hipparchus of Nicaea

claims.text: Hipparchus discovered the precession of the equinoxes.
He compiled a star catalogue of around 850 stars and a magnitude scale.
He constructed the first known trigonometric chord table.
The Antikythera mechanism implements a lunar theory derived from Hipparchus.

summary: The founder of scientific astronomy, who discovered the precession of the equinoxes and compiled the first comprehensive star catalogue.
significance: Introduced quantitative prediction and trigonometry into astronomy; Ptolemy's Almagest rests almost entirely on his work.
body:
By comparing his own measurements of stellar positions with Babylonian records over centuries, Hipparchus detected that the equinoxes shift slowly against the fixed stars — precession, a cycle of about 26,000 years caused by the wobble of Earth's axis. Detecting a drift of roughly one degree per century with pre-telescopic instruments is a remarkable achievement.

He catalogued around 850 stars with positions and brightness, and his magnitude scale — brightest as first magnitude — is still in use. He built the first trigonometric table, a chord table, making astronomy computational.

The Antikythera mechanism's lunar gearing implements a variable-speed model of the Moon consistent with his theory, which suggests his work was being engineered into bronze within a century of his death.

name: Zeno of Citium

claims.text: Zeno founded the Stoic school at Athens around 300 BC.
Stoicism holds that virtue is the only genuine good.
Zeno's own writings are lost and known only through quotation.

summary: Founder of Stoicism, which taught that virtue is the only good and that we should distinguish what is in our power from what is not.
significance: Stoicism became the dominant philosophy of the Roman elite and remains the most widely practised ancient philosophy today.
body:
Zeno was a Phoenician merchant from Cyprus who was shipwrecked near Athens, wandered into a bookshop, read about Socrates, and stayed. He taught in the Stoa Poikile — the Painted Porch — from which Stoicism takes its name.

The core claim is that virtue alone is good, vice alone is bad, and everything else — health, wealth, reputation, life itself — is "indifferent", though some indifferents are naturally preferred. Since only our own judgements are fully in our power, tranquillity comes from aligning our will with nature rather than with outcomes.

His works are lost; Stoicism survives through Roman successors — Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius. The Athenians gave him a public burial, an unusual honour for a foreign resident.

name: Epicurus

claims.text: Epicurus founded a philosophical community at Athens admitting women and slaves.
His physics was atomist and materialist, derived from Democritus.
He argued that death should not be feared because it involves no experience.
The Herculaneum papyri preserve Epicurean philosophical works.

summary: Atomist philosopher who taught that pleasure — properly understood as tranquillity and freedom from fear — is the goal of life.
significance: Defended a fully materialist account of the world, and argued that fear of death and the gods is groundless and removable.
body:
Epicurus founded a community called the Garden outside Athens, admitting women and slaves as members — unusual to the point of scandal. His physics is atomist, taken from Democritus: everything is atoms and void, the soul is material and disperses at death, and the gods exist but take no interest in us.

His ethics follows from this. "Death is nothing to us" — where death is, we are not. The pleasure he recommends is not indulgence but the absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance, best achieved through friendship, simple food and philosophy. The popular use of "epicurean" to mean luxurious inverts what he actually taught; his enemies started that.

Almost all his writings are lost. Carbonised scrolls from the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum contain Epicurean texts, and are now being read by machine learning without unrolling them.

name: Cleopatra VII

claims.text: Cleopatra VII was the last Ptolemaic ruler of Egypt.
She was of Macedonian Greek descent.
She allied with Julius Caesar and later Mark Antony.
She died in Alexandria in 30 BC shortly after Antony.
She learned the Egyptian language, unlike her predecessors.
She died from the bite of an asp.

summary: The last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, whose alliances with Caesar and Antony were a strategy for Egyptian independence — and who lost.
significance: Her death in 30 BC ends the Hellenistic age and the last Greek-ruled successor kingdom of Alexander.
body:
Cleopatra was Macedonian Greek by descent, not Egyptian, and ruled a kingdom founded by Alexander's general. She was reportedly the first of her dynasty in three centuries to learn Egyptian, and Plutarch says she spoke many languages and rarely needed an interpreter.

Her relationships with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony are usually told as romance, and were unmistakably policy: Egypt was rich and militarily weak, and the only way to survive was to be indispensable to whoever held power in Rome. It worked for twenty years.

After Actium in 31 BC she and Antony were finished. She died in August 30 BC. Plutarch reports the asp but notes that no one knows what actually happened; some modern historians favour a poison draught, and the snake may be part of the imagery Octavian's propaganda encouraged. Egypt became a Roman province directly under the emperor.

name: Polybius

claims.text: Polybius was taken to Rome as an Achaean hostage in 167 BC.
He witnessed the destruction of Carthage in 146 BC.
He analysed the Roman constitution as a mixture of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy.
His account of the legion-versus-phalanx contrast is broadly reliable.

summary: Greek statesman deported to Rome as a hostage, who wrote the definitive analysis of how Rome conquered the Mediterranean.
significance: Explained Roman success through institutions rather than luck, and his theory of the mixed constitution influenced Montesquieu and the American founders.
body:
Polybius was one of a thousand Achaean hostages taken to Rome in 167 BC. He became close to Scipio Aemilianus and was present at the destruction of Carthage in 146 BC, where he reports Scipio weeping and quoting Homer on the fall of Troy.

His *Histories* set out to explain how Rome subdued the known world in fifty-three years. His answer is constitutional: Rome mixed monarchy (consuls), aristocracy (senate) and democracy (assemblies) so that each checked the others, producing stability where pure forms decayed. He also gives the clearest technical comparison of legion and phalanx.

He insisted history must be written by people with political and military experience, and criticised armchair historians sharply — which, having watched a world order end from inside, he had earned.

name: Pyrrhus of Epirus

claims.text: Pyrrhus defeated Roman armies at Heraclea (280 BC) and Asculum (279 BC) with heavy losses.
The phrase "Pyrrhic victory" derives from his remark after Asculum.
He died at Argos in 272 BC.

summary: King of Epirus and one of antiquity's finest tacticians, whose costly victories over Rome gave us the phrase "Pyrrhic victory".
significance: His campaigns were Rome's first encounter with a Hellenistic army, and revealed that Roman manpower could absorb defeats no Greek kingdom could.
body:
Pyrrhus was a cousin of Alexander through Olympias, and Hannibal reportedly ranked him among the greatest commanders. Invited by Tarentum to defend Greek Italy against Rome, he won at Heraclea in 280 BC and Asculum in 279, both times with elephants the Romans had never faced.

Both wins cost him irreplaceable veterans. Plutarch reports his remark after Asculum that another such victory would ruin him. Rome simply raised more legions.

He campaigned in Sicily, returned to Italy, was fought to a standstill at Beneventum in 275, and went home. He died in a street fight in Argos in 272 BC, reportedly stunned by a roof tile thrown by an old woman and killed where he fell.

name: Antiochus III the Great

claims.text: Antiochus III restored Seleucid control over the eastern provinces in a campaign of 212–205 BC.
He was defeated by Rome at Magnesia in 190 BC.
The Treaty of Apamea stripped the Seleucids of Anatolia and imposed a massive indemnity.
He sheltered Hannibal at his court.

summary: Seleucid king who restored his empire from Anatolia to Bactria, then lost it all by provoking Rome.
significance: His defeat at Magnesia in 190 BC made Rome the arbiter of the eastern Mediterranean.
body:
Antiochus inherited a fragmenting empire at eighteen and spent a decade recovering it, marching east to Bactria and India in a campaign consciously modelled on Alexander's — which earned him the title "the Great".

He then crossed into Greece, and Rome responded. Defeated at Thermopylae in 191 BC and decisively at Magnesia in 190, he accepted the Treaty of Apamea: he surrendered Anatolia, gave up his elephants and fleet, and agreed to an indemnity so large it destabilised his finances for a generation. He was killed while looting a temple to raise money for it.

He had also given refuge to Hannibal, which Rome did not forget.

name: Philip V of Macedon

claims.text: Philip V allied with Hannibal against Rome in 215 BC.
He was defeated at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC.
The terrain at Cynoscephalae prevented the phalanx from forming a continuous line.

summary: Antigonid king whose alliance with Hannibal drew Rome into Greece, and whose defeat at Cynoscephalae ended Macedonian supremacy.
significance: His reign is the hinge on which Greece passes from Hellenistic self-determination to Roman control.
body:
Philip V allied with Hannibal after Cannae in 215 BC, hoping to expel Rome from Illyria while it was occupied. The First Macedonian War was indecisive, but it made Macedon a permanent Roman concern.

At Cynoscephalae in 197 BC his phalanx was caught deploying on broken hilly ground. Half of it formed and drove the Roman left back; the other half was still in march column when the Roman right rolled over it, and an unnamed tribune took twenty maniples into the exposed rear of the successful wing. Polybius drew the general lesson: the phalanx is irresistible on level ground and helpless without it.

Rome left him his throne. His son Perseus tried again and lost at Pydna in 168 BC, ending the kingdom.

name: Mithridates VI of Pontus

claims.text: Mithridates VI ordered a coordinated massacre of Romans in Asia Minor in 88 BC.
Sulla sacked Athens in 86 BC after it sided with Mithridates.
He fought three wars against Rome and was defeated by Pompey.
He made himself immune to poison by taking sub-lethal doses.

summary: King of Pontus who mounted the last great challenge to Rome in the Greek East, ordering the massacre of tens of thousands of Romans in one day.
significance: Fought Rome for four decades across three wars, and his defeat completed Roman control of Anatolia and the Aegean.
body:
In 88 BC Mithridates orchestrated the Asiatic Vespers: a coordinated massacre of Roman and Italian residents across the cities of Asia Minor, with ancient estimates of 80,000 killed in a single day. The figure is probably inflated; the coordination is not in doubt.

Many Greek cities, including Athens, sided with him against Roman tax farmers. Sulla besieged and sacked Athens in 86 BC in response, damaging the city severely.

Three wars followed. Pompey finally broke him in 66 BC. Cornered by his own son's rebellion, he tried to poison himself and failed — he had reportedly spent his life taking small doses of poisons to build immunity, which is the origin of the word *mithridatism* — and had a bodyguard kill him instead.

name: Croesus

claims.text: Lydia under the Mermnad dynasty produced the earliest standardised coinage.
Croesus was defeated by Cyrus the Great around 546 BC.
Croesus made rich dedications at Delphi.
Croesus met Solon.

summary: Last king of Lydia, proverbially rich, who tested the oracles and destroyed his own empire by trusting one.
significance: His kingdom minted the first true coinage, and his fall to Cyrus brought Persia to the Aegean coast and into contact with the Greeks.
body:
Herodotus makes Croesus the subject of his first extended narrative. He tested the oracles by asking each what he was doing on a set day; only Delphi answered correctly. He then asked whether to attack Persia and was told he would destroy a great empire. He attacked, and destroyed his own.

Herodotus also gives him a meeting with Solon, who declines to call him the happiest of men because no life can be judged until it has ended. The chronology makes the meeting impossible, and Herodotus almost certainly knew that — the story is doing moral rather than reportorial work.

Lydia under Croesus and his predecessors produced the first standardised coins, initially of electrum and then of refined gold and silver, an innovation Greek cities adopted almost immediately.

name: Cyrus the Great

claims.text: Cyrus founded the Achaemenid Empire and conquered Media, Lydia and Babylon.
The Cyrus Cylinder records his settlement of Babylon in 539 BC.
Persian conquest of Lydia brought the Ionian Greek cities under Persian rule.
The Cyrus Cylinder is an early charter of human rights.

summary: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire, who conquered Media, Lydia and Babylon and established a template of tolerant imperial rule.
significance: Created the empire that would dominate Greek foreign policy for two centuries and that Alexander eventually destroyed.
body:
Cyrus built the largest empire the world had yet seen in about twenty years. His conquest of Lydia in 546 BC brought Persian rule to the Ionian Greek cities, making conflict with the Greek mainland a structural certainty.

He governed by conciliating rather than erasing. The Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian foundation text, presents him as restoring temples and returning displaced peoples — including, in the biblical account, permitting Jewish exiles to return and rebuild the Temple. It is a royal inscription and therefore propaganda, but it matches an evident practical policy of local accommodation.

Greeks regarded him with respect: Xenophon wrote an idealised education of Cyrus as a manual of ideal kingship, and Alexander made a point of restoring his tomb at Pasargadae after finding it plundered.

name: Darius I

claims.text: Darius I reorganised the Achaemenid Empire into satrapies with fixed tribute.
The Behistun inscription records his account of his accession in three languages.
Behistun provided the key to deciphering cuneiform.
A Persian force was defeated by the Athenians at Marathon in 490 BC.

summary: Achaemenid king who organised the empire into satrapies, built Persepolis and the Royal Road, and lost at Marathon.
significance: His administrative system held an empire of perhaps 25 million people together, and his invasion of Greece began the Persian Wars.
body:
Darius took power in 522 BC after a disputed succession he justified at length in the trilingual Behistun inscription, carved 100 metres up a cliff — the text that gave nineteenth-century scholars the key to cuneiform.

He divided the empire into about twenty satrapies with fixed tribute, standardised coinage with the gold daric, and built the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, along which relay couriers covered 2,700 km in a week. Herodotus' description of them is the source of the unofficial motto of the US Postal Service.

The Ionian Revolt of 499 BC, supported by Athens and Eretria, provoked his intervention in Greece. His punitive expedition was defeated at Marathon in 490 BC. He died preparing a larger invasion, which his son Xerxes carried out.

name: Xerxes I

claims.text: Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BC with a large combined army and fleet.
Persian forces captured and burned the Athenian Acropolis in 480 BC.
The Athos canal was actually excavated, as geophysical survey has confirmed.
He was assassinated in a court conspiracy in 465 BC.
Herodotus' figures of over a million invaders are credible.

summary: Achaemenid king who led the greatest invasion of Greece in 480 BC, burned Athens, and lost his fleet at Salamis.
significance: His defeat preserved Greek independence at the moment when Classical Athens was about to emerge.
body:
Xerxes assembled an army and fleet of unprecedented size, bridged the Hellespont with pontoons of lashed ships, and cut a canal through the Athos peninsula — a feat Greeks thought boastful and which modern geophysical survey has confirmed was actually built.

After Thermopylae he took Athens and burned the Acropolis. Then at Salamis the Greek fleet, fighting in narrows chosen by Themistocles, destroyed his naval superiority. He returned to Asia, leaving Mardonius to be defeated at Plataea in 479 BC.

Herodotus portrays him as a study in hubris — whipping the sea for wrecking his bridge — but Persian sources present a conventional, effective king who completed Persepolis. He was assassinated in a palace conspiracy in 465 BC.

name: Darius III

claims.text: Darius III was defeated by Alexander at Issus (333 BC) and Gaugamela (331 BC).
His family was captured after Issus and treated well by Alexander.
He was murdered by the satrap Bessus in 330 BC.
He was a weak or cowardly commander.

summary: The last Achaemenid king, defeated by Alexander at Issus and Gaugamela and murdered by his own satrap.
significance: His defeat ended the two-century Achaemenid Empire and transferred the Near East to Macedonian rule.
body:
Darius III came to the throne in 336 BC, the same year as Alexander, after a court poisoning cleared the way. He faced an invasion two years later.

At Issus in 333 BC his larger army was caught in terrain too narrow to deploy in; he fled the field, leaving his mother, wife and children to be captured — Alexander treated them with conspicuous respect. He offered enormous territorial concessions twice and was refused both times. At Gaugamela in 331 he chose open ground and levelled it for his scythed chariots, and still lost when Alexander drove a wedge into a gap opened in the Persian line.

He fled east and was arrested and stabbed by his satrap Bessus. Alexander found him dying or dead, and had him buried at Persepolis with royal honours, then hunted Bessus down and executed him — establishing himself as the legitimate avenger rather than merely the conqueror.

name: Porus

claims.text: Alexander defeated Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BC.
Porus was reinstated as ruler of his territory under Macedonian overlordship.
The "as a king" exchange occurred as reported.

summary: Indian king who fought Alexander at the Hydaspes with war elephants, lost, and was reinstated as a satrap.
significance: His resistance marked the effective eastern limit of Alexander's conquest and produced one of the most quoted exchanges in ancient history.
body:
Porus met Alexander at the Hydaspes in 326 BC with around 200 elephants and a large army, on the far bank of a river swollen by monsoon rain. Alexander crossed upstream at night in a storm, concealing the move with repeated feints. The battle was the hardest of his career; the elephants panicked and trampled troops on both sides.

Captured and brought before Alexander, Porus was asked how he wished to be treated. He answered: as a king. Alexander restored his kingdom and enlarged it.

The practical reason is as important as the gesture — Alexander needed a strong local ruler to hold the region, and Porus was the obvious candidate. The battle also killed Bucephalus, and Alexander founded a city in his horse's name.

name: Ramesses III

claims.text: Ramesses III repelled land and sea invasions by the Sea Peoples in his eighth year.
The Medinet Habu reliefs name several Sea Peoples groups.
CT scanning shows his throat was cut, consistent with the harem conspiracy.
The Peleset are the Philistines of the Hebrew Bible.

summary: Egyptian pharaoh who repelled the Sea Peoples in the 1170s BC and recorded the campaigns on the walls of Medinet Habu.
significance: His inscriptions are the single most important written source for the Bronze Age Collapse.
body:
The Medinet Habu reliefs depict land and naval battles against a coalition Ramesses names — Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh — and describe them as having already swept away Hatti, Alashiya, Carchemish and Arzawa. That list matches the archaeological destruction horizon closely.

The naval battle scene is the earliest detailed depiction of a sea fight anywhere, showing Egyptian archers destroying ships trapped against the shore.

Egypt survived but was permanently weakened; a documented strike by tomb workers at Deir el-Medina over unpaid grain rations shows the strain. Ramesses himself was killed in a harem conspiracy — CT scanning of his mummy in 2012 revealed a deep cut to the throat.

name: Heinrich Schliemann

claims.text: Schliemann excavated at Hisarlik (Troy) from 1871 and at Mycenae in 1876.
He discovered the Mycenae shaft graves and their gold funerary masks.
His excavation methods destroyed substantial stratigraphic evidence at Troy.
Several of his published accounts contain fabricated details.
"Priam's Treasure" belongs to the era of the Trojan War.

summary: German businessman who excavated Troy and Mycenae, proved the Bronze Age Aegean was real, and destroyed a great deal of it doing so.
significance: Founded Aegean prehistory as a field, and stands as its permanent cautionary tale about method and self-promotion.
body:
Schliemann made a fortune in indigo and Californian gold, then went looking for Homer's cities. At Hisarlik from 1871 he dug a vast trench straight down through the mound, destroying much of the layer that was actually Homeric-era Troy in order to reach a much older one he called "Priam's Treasure".

At Mycenae in 1876 he found the shaft graves with their gold masks, and telegraphed that he had gazed on the face of Agamemnon. He had not — the burials are roughly three centuries too early — but the discovery was genuinely epochal: it proved a rich Bronze Age civilisation had existed on the Greek mainland.

His published accounts are unreliable. He embellished, backdated discoveries, and by his own account had his Greek wife Sophia present when she was elsewhere. The dig, the find and the story have to be assessed separately.

name: Sir Arthur Evans

claims.text: Evans excavated Knossos from 1900 and named the Minoan civilisation.
He reconstructed portions of the palace in reinforced concrete.
Several restored frescoes at Knossos incorporate substantial modern invention.
He rejected the possibility that Linear B recorded Greek.
The reconstructions did more harm than good to understanding of the site.

summary: Excavator of Knossos, who named the Minoan civilisation and reconstructed its palace in painted concrete.
significance: Revealed Europe's earliest civilisation — and shaped how it is seen through reconstructions that are substantially his own interpretation.
body:
Evans bought the Kephala mound and began digging in 1900. Within weeks he had uncovered frescoes, storage magazines and clay tablets in two unknown scripts. He named the civilisation "Minoan" after the legendary king Minos, and identified the complex with the labyrinth of the Minotaur myth.

His "reconstitutions" used reinforced concrete to rebuild columns, staircases and upper storeys, and commissioned Émile Gilliéron and his son to restore frescoes from fragments — sometimes from very few fragments. The famous "Prince of the Lilies" combines pieces that may not belong to one figure, or even to one sex. Visitors to Knossos are looking at an Edwardian interpretation as much as a Bronze Age building.

Against that: he excavated carefully by the standards of his day, published in detail, and preserved the site. He also insisted, correctly, that the Linear B tablets were an administrative archive — while wrongly refusing to accept that the language could be Greek.

name: Michael Ventris

claims.text: Ventris deciphered Linear B in 1952 and identified its language as Greek.
His grid method organised signs by shared consonants and vowels without assuming sound values.
Cretan place names provided the crucial test of the decipherment.
He expected the language to be Etruscan-related, not Greek.

summary: The architect who deciphered Linear B in 1952, proving that Mycenaean Greeks wrote Greek five centuries before Homer.
significance: One of the great intellectual achievements of the twentieth century, and the single most important advance in Aegean prehistory.
body:
Ventris heard Evans lecture at fourteen and asked whether the tablets had been read. They had not. He worked on the problem for years alongside a career in architecture, circulating "Work Notes" to other scholars — an unusually open method for a decipherment.
